fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me, Ravid. It's a question I've thought about a lot, partly because my own career has sort of tracked the shift in how the community answers it.

When I started, around DenseNet, the answer felt obvious. Architecture was the main lever. You'd come up with a new connectivity pattern or a new block, you'd gain a few points on ImageNet, and that was a paper. The implicit belief was that the inductive biases you build into the network are what determine what it can learn.

I think that belief has been mostly, but not entirely, overturned. The ConvNeXt work was actually what convinced me. We took a plain ResNet and basically just modernized the training recipe and a few design details, step by step, and ended up matching Swin Transformers. The interesting part wasn't that ConvNets are secretly better. It was that most of the gap people attributed to "attention versus convolution" was really about training procedure, data augmentation, normalization choices, things that aren't architecture in the sense people usually mean. So the honest takeaway was that architecture matters less than we thought, and the specific flavor of architecture matters even less once you're at scale with enough data.

That said, I'd push back on the strong version of "architecture doesn't matter," which you hear a lot now. I'd phrase it differently. Architecture choice today is less about what the model can represent and more about what the model can be trained to do efficiently on the hardware we actually have. The transformer won not because it has the right inductive bias for language or vision. It won because it's extremely parallelizable, it scales predictably, and the whole ecosystem of kernels and infrastructure got optimized around it. That's a real architectural property, it's just not the kind we used to write papers about.

So for making AI useful, I'd say two things. First, for the big frontier models, architecture is close to settled, and the leverage is in data, scale, and post-training. If you're a researcher, spending your time on a slightly better attention variant is probably not where the impact is. Second, and this is the part I still find exciting, for the long tail of deployment, where you have latency budgets, memory constraints, edge devices, or you want a model that's actually understandable, architecture still matters a lot. Efficiency, sparsity, how the network compresses, those are architectural questions, and that's where a lot of my group's work sits now.

The one thing I'd caution against is assuming the current convergence is permanent. We converged on transformers under a particular set of hardware constraints and a particular data regime. If either of those shifts, I wouldn't be shocked if architecture becomes a first-class variable again.

opus-5.5.text:
That's a question I think about a lot, partly because my own research history has gone back and forth on it.

Early in my PhD I worked on DenseNet, and at that time the general feeling in the field was that architecture was everything. If you designed a better way to connect layers, you got a big jump on ImageNet, and that was how progress happened. A lot of the community's energy went into designing new blocks and new connectivity patterns.

Over time my view has become more nuanced. One project that changed my thinking was ConvNeXt. When Vision Transformers came out, the common narrative was that attention is fundamentally better than convolution for vision. What we found was that if you take a standard ResNet and gradually modernize it, adopting the training recipe, macro design choices, larger kernels, different normalization and activation choices, you can close most or all of the gap with transformers. So a large part of what looked like an architectural advantage was really about training techniques, data, and scale, which had co-evolved with the new architecture.

So my current view is roughly this. Among reasonable, well-tuned architectures, the specific choice matters less than people often assume for final accuracy at a given scale. Data, the training objective, compute, and how you scale tend to dominate. You see this with language models too. The core transformer hasn't changed dramatically over the years, and most of the gains have come from scaling and from data.

But I wouldn't say architecture doesn't matter. It matters in a few ways that are very important for usefulness.

First, efficiency. How expensive is it to train and to run at inference time? How does cost grow with sequence length or resolution? That determines what you can deploy and what you can afford to scale up.

Second, scalability and stability. Some architectures are much easier to scale without training blowing up, and they have good properties under parallel hardware. The transformer's big win wasn't necessarily higher accuracy at small scale. It was that it scales very gracefully and maps well onto GPUs.

Third, generality. An architecture that handles text, images, video, and actions in a unified way makes it much easier to build multimodal systems, and that's a big part of what makes AI useful in practice.

So I'd say architecture is less of a magic ingredient for raw capability than we once believed, but it's still a crucial enabler. It decides how far and how cheaply you can push the things that actually drive capability. It's also worth periodically questioning components we take for granted. For example, we recently looked at whether normalization layers are really necessary in transformers, and it turns out you can replace them with something quite simple. Some pieces we treat as essential may just be historical habits.

fable-5.text:
Thanks for having me, Ravid. That's a question I think about a lot, and my answer has actually evolved over the years.

I'd say architecture matters, but maybe not in the way people usually assume. A lot of my research, including the ConvNeXt work, was really about testing this: we took a standard ConvNet and asked, if we give it the same modern training recipes and design refinements that Transformers enjoy, how far does the gap actually close? And the answer was, mostly, it closes. Much of what people attributed to the attention mechanism itself turned out to come from training procedures, data, and scale. So in terms of raw accuracy on a benchmark, I think the specific architecture family is less decisive than the field sometimes believes. Different architectures, trained well, often converge to surprisingly similar performance and even learn similar representations.

But that doesn't mean architecture is unimportant for making AI useful — it just shifts where the importance lies. Architecture choice really matters for things like efficiency, hardware compatibility, and scalability. Transformers won in large part because they map so well onto modern accelerators and scale predictably with data and compute. If you're deploying models on a phone, or serving billions of queries, the architecture determines your latency, your memory footprint, your cost. Those are the constraints that decide whether AI is actually useful in practice, not just whether it tops a leaderboard.

So my overall view is: for capability, be a bit skeptical when a new architecture claims a breakthrough — control for training and data first, because the baseline is often undertrained. For usefulness, pay a lot of attention to architecture, because that's where efficiency and deployability are decided. Simplicity also matters more than people give it credit for. The architectures that endure tend to be the simple, general ones that the whole community can build on.

opus-5.text:
I have a somewhat contrarian view on this, which is that architecture gets more credit than it deserves for where we are today.

If you look back at the last decade, a lot of what we attributed to architectural innovation turned out to be training recipes, data, and scale in disguise. We did this study where we took a plain ConvNet and just modernized the training procedure — the augmentations, the optimizer, the schedule, larger kernels — and a lot of the gap people believed was intrinsic to attention mechanisms just closed. That was ConvNeXt. The lesson I took from it wasn't "ConvNets are better." It was that when you compare two architectures, you are almost never comparing two architectures. You're comparing two research communities' accumulated tuning effort.

So where does architecture actually matter? I think it matters most where you're constrained. If you have limited data, the inductive bias you build in is doing real work, because it's substituting for examples you don't have. And it matters enormously for efficiency — what you can serve, what fits in memory, how the thing maps onto hardware. Transformers won partly because they parallelize well on GPUs, which is an engineering fact, not a statement about intelligence.

But for raw capability at scale? I suspect many reasonable architectures land in roughly the same place. The interesting question for usefulness is almost always the data.

sonnet-5.5.text:
I think architecture matters, but less than people usually assume, and it matters in a different way than the common story suggests.

When you control for the training recipe, the data, and the scale, many architectures end up much closer in accuracy than the papers around them implied. My own experience with modernizing ConvNets pointed that way. A lot of what looked like an architectural advantage was really better training recipes, more data, or better optimization. So if the question is which design makes a model fundamentally smarter, I'd say data and training objectives usually dominate.

But "architecture doesn't matter" goes too far. It matters a lot for efficiency: how much compute you need to reach a given quality, how well the model uses the hardware, how it scales with sequence length, and how cheap inference is. Those things decide whether a capability can be deployed widely or stays a demo. A change that gives you the same quality at half the cost is a real change in how useful AI is, even if it doesn't raise the ceiling.

There's also path dependence. The Transformer has been dominant for years, partly because it's good, but also because the whole ecosystem of hardware, kernels, and tooling grew up around it. That makes it hard for alternatives to win, and the bar for replacing it is high. So I'd look for architectural progress in simplification and efficiency, not in a dramatic new design that suddenly unlocks intelligence.

haiku-5.5.text:
I think architecture matters less for usefulness than people often assume. For years the field treated the backbone as the main lever, and we kept tweaking attention patterns and block designs. In my own work on ConvNeXt, a lot of the gains that looked like they came from clever new blocks actually came from better training recipes, more data, and more careful scaling. Once you modernize the training setup, a plain, well-understood architecture goes surprisingly far.

I don't want to dismiss it entirely, though. Architecture strongly affects how efficiently a model uses compute and memory, and usefulness is partly about cost and latency. A design that's a bit better on a benchmark but much slower to serve may not be more useful to anyone. So architecture sets how efficiently a model can learn and run, but the data, the training objective, and post-training largely determine whether it behaves the way people need.

Where I think the leverage is for usefulness right now is less in the backbone and more in how we train and align these systems, and in building evaluations that show whether they're doing what we want. Architecture is important, but it's one part of a larger system, and I think the community overweights it partly because it's the easiest part to write a paper about.

astra-6.text:
I think architecture is important, but I would judge it by what it enables. Does it let us learn more effectively from the data we have? Does it make training or inference cheaper? Does it make the model easier to use under practical constraints? Those improvements can matter a lot for making AI useful, even if they don’t produce a dramatic increase on a benchmark.

At the same time, architecture is one part of the system. You have to consider it together with the data, the training procedure, and the compute budget. An architecture that works well in one setting might not be the best choice in another.

So I wouldn’t frame the goal as finding a universally best architecture. I’d ask: for this task, with these resources, what design gives us the most useful model?

sol-6.1.text:
I think architecture is important, but it’s one part of the whole system. You also have the data, the training procedure, and the amount of computation you can use. So when we compare two architectures, we have to be careful: are we seeing a benefit from the architecture itself, or did one model get a better training recipe or more compute?

For making AI useful, I think a very important role of architecture is efficiency. It’s not just whether you can get a slightly better number on a benchmark. Can you achieve the same capability with less computation? Can you run the model with less memory, or respond faster? Those differences can determine whether someone can actually use the model in their application.

So I wouldn’t say architecture is everything, and I wouldn’t say it doesn’t matter. The question is what constraint you’re trying to address. A good architectural idea should make it easier to learn the capabilities we want, within the resources we have.

For a long time, we searched for a single clever architecture that would suddenly make models much better. What we see now is that scale, data, and optimization can make relatively simple architectures extraordinarily capable. But architecture determines the efficiency frontier: how much compute, memory, and data you need to get a certain capability. That matters enormously if we want AI to be useful broadly rather than only in a few giant data centers. So I would say it is less about finding a magical new model, and more about designing systems that can learn and run efficiently in the real world.

luna-5.6.text: Architecture choice is important, but I would not treat it as the single decisive factor. A good architecture gives the model the right inductive biases: it can make learning more efficient, improve how the system handles structure and context, and reduce the computational cost of producing useful behavior. So I think of architecture as a major lever for making AI more capable and efficient, while usefulness ultimately depends on the whole system rather than on the architecture alone.
